title: std::array

youtube.title: C++ std::array: A Safer Array | C++ Programming EP 34
youtube.description: In this episode you will make a std array, use size and at and read an out-of-range error, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:16 std::array · 1:26 A std array · 2:25 Plain array or std::array · 3:10 Second program · 4:30 Recap · 5:00 Bug of the Day · 6:00 Challenge · 6:26 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "STD::ARRAY" in tomato on butter; Xecxec next to an array with a safety helmet; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to an array with a safety helmet

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet std array. It is a normal array with a safety helmet. It knows its size, and it can check your index.

scenes.onScreen: "std::array": numbered lines (1. std array knows its own size; 2. at checks the index; 3. It costs nothing extra) and an analogy card: a locker row with a guard: ask for door nine, and the guard says no such door
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: The std array type wraps a plain array. It knows its own size. The size function tells you. The at function checks the index. If the index is wrong, it stops with an error. A plain array does not check anything, and a wrong index gives garbage. Think of a locker row with a guard. If you ask for door nine, the guard says there is no such door. A plain array is fast, but it is careless. It does not know its own size, and it does not check the index. The std array fixes both problems and costs nothing extra. The size is part of the type. So array of int, three, and array of int, four, are different types.
points: std array knows its own size

analogy.title: std::array
analogy.body: A locker row with a guard: ask for door nine, and the guard says no such door

scenes.onScreen: stdarray.cpp: size, at and fill on a std array
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The array header gives us std array. [HL 6] The type and the size go in angle brackets. [HL 7] The size is three. [HL 8] At one gives the second item, which is six. [HL 9] The fill function sets every item to zero. [HL 10] So the last item is now zero. [HL 6] The two parts inside the angle brackets are the item type and the size. [HL 7] The size function tells us the size. No need to count by hand. [HL 8] The at function checks the index, and it stops the program with an error if the index is too big. [HL 9] The fill function sets every item to one value, here zero.

scenes.onScreen: a table that compares the two
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here are the two types side by side. The std array knows its size. It can check an index with at. You can copy it with a single equals sign. And it costs no more memory than a plain array. Notice the difference in the table. Square brackets are fast but trust you. The at function costs a tiny check, and it protects you. While you learn, use at, and you will find your mistakes sooner.

diagram.caption: a table that compares the two

scenes.onScreen: same.cpp: two std arrays compared with two equals signs
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] This line copies the whole array. A plain array cannot do this. [HL 8] We change the first item of b only. [HL 9] Two equals signs compare all items. The arrays differ now, so the answer is false. [HL 10] The original a still starts with one, and b starts with nine. [HL 7] A std array can be copied with a plain equals sign. A plain array cannot. The copy has its own items, so a change to b leaves a alone. [HL 9] You can also compare two arrays with the double equals sign. Here, they differ, so the answer is false.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as same dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints false, and then one and nine. Notice that a keeps its first item. The copy changed, but the original did not.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Std array wraps a plain array. Two. It knows its own size. Three. At checks the index and stops on a wrong one. Four. You can copy and compare two std arrays. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Std array wraps a plain array.
At checks the index and stops on a wrong one.
You can copy and compare two std arrays.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: An index that is too big
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program crashes and the run-time error appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The array has three items, and we ask for index five. At stops the program. It says terminate called after throwing an instance of out of range. That is better than reading garbage. Check the index against the size before you use it. Indexes run from zero to size minus one. The index nine is far outside a row of three. A plain array would read some random memory and say nothing. The at function stops the program, and the message tells you what went wrong.

scenes.onScreen: Std array put on a helmet. Now it has a safe place to fall.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Std array put on a helmet. Now it has a safe place to fall.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: fill and print a std array
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make a std array of four ints. Fill it with the number seven. Print every item with a range-based for. Hint: the fill function sets every item to one value, so call it once. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: std vector. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program error output (exactly as the program prints it):

terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'
  what():  array::at: __n (which is 5) >= _Nm (which is 3)
bug.why: The array has three items, so the valid indexes are zero, one and two. At stops the program with an exception instead of reading garbage.

challengeAnswer: Write array of int, four. Call fill with seven. Then use for int x colon the array, and print x.
